newsitem.title: TURKEY: Import curbs dominate Turkish grain gathering.
newsitem.headline: Import curbs dominate Turkish grain gathering.

text.p: A clampdown on imports will dominate an international grain conference in Turkey from Monday after the country's Islamist-led government acted to protect local farmers, traders said on Sunday.
Turkey said on Saturday it was raising import taxes for corn (maize) and wheat five-fold to 15 percent from three percent due to an increase in Turkish grain output this year.
"We have to protect our farmers and our grain industry," Mahmut Arslan, president of the Arbel trading company, said on the eve of a second annual conference at the Mediterranean resort of Antalya.
Others, however, said the decision would hit local users of corn as well as pasta exporters. Some depend on importing pasta-making durum wheat to boost quality from local crops.
Turkey is the world's second largest pasta exporter after Italy. It produces about half a million tonnes annually and exported 115,000 tonnes last year.
Pasta makers say they will tighten their belts and keep importing foreign durum wheat, despite the higher duties which are likely to cost them some $30 per tonne.
"We have to import because local wheat is not satisfactory," a senior pasta industry official said as word of the imminent import tax decision spread last week.
Supplies could come from Mexico, the United States, Spain, Canada or France, he said.
Turkey has said it expects a bumper harvest for all kinds of wheat, including durum, of some 18 million tonnes this year, up from 15.5 million in 1995.
Grain import levies were slashed two years ago to encourage imports in the wake of what were then disappointing crops.

Traders say Turkey also imported corn in the past three years and the government move on levies will adversely affect local industries that use corn. These include pop-corn makers and makers of fructose for the food and beverage industry.
"Turkey imports about 800,000 to 900,000 tonnes of corn every year. I don't know what the sector will do now," a Western trader based in Turkey said.

The government of Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, who formed a coalition with conservatives in July, has vowed not to let cheaper corn enter the Turkish market and threaten the country's farmers. The government subsidies corn purchases from domestic farmers at about 30 percent above the world price.
Turkish Farm Minister Musa Demirci will inaugurate the three-day Antalya conference, a large part of which is expected to focus on the concerns of pasta makers and other importers.
